This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Louise Givoni.
Federal investigators are looking into cyberattacks
against dozens of commercial shipping festivals bound
for U.S. ports and the possibility
that the attacks are linked to Iran.
A U.S. official tells NPR an Iranian role
in these episodes is strongly suspected.
NPR's Jenna McLaughlin reports.
In August, FBI and Coast Guard teams boarded two different
vessels to investigate intrusions into their systems
and secure the ships before they were allowed
to enter U.S. ports.
But the cybersecurity threat could be much more widespread.
According to a U.S. official familiar with the matter
who spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity,
the U.S. government is tracking as many
as 50 foreign commercial ships, including energy tankers,
that they believe have been compromised by hackers.
The U.S. official told NPR that the bad actors took advantage
of known vulnerabilities and managed to get inside some
of these ships' operational technology systems,
meaning they could have taken over control of steering,
navigation, cargo management, and other processes.
It could be yet another front in the U.S. war with Iran.
Jenna McLaughlin, NPR News.
>> President Trump is leading the cheering
for Jensen Wong's return as CEO of NVIDIA,
but not everyone is pleased, and NPR's Andrea Hsu reports.
>> Unfathomable, a backslide.
>> Those are words that some are using to describe the decision
by NVIDIA's board to reinstate Wong after finding him
in violation of the company's code of conduct.
Frieda Kaper Klein has long used her role as an investor
to promote diversity and inclusion in Silicon Valley.
She says Wong's swift comeback sends a troubling message.
>> You can violate corporate policy.
You can possibly threaten national security.
You can make up your own rules as you go.
As long as you bring in the money.
>> Videos posted to social media show Wong arriving
at company headquarters to loud applause.
He tells the crowd he'll be a better CEO the second time
around, Andrea Hsu, NPR News.
>> On the south lawn of the White House today,
President Trump gave thanksgiving pardons to two turkeys
from West Virginia named Freedom and Feathers,
and PR's Franco Ordonez has details.
>> President Trump said the two large white birds,
born in July, grew in leaps and bounds
and now weigh a combined 82 pounds.
>> Following today's pardon, Freedom and Feathers will travel
to Texas and will live out their days in solitude and peace.
>> The president used the event
to also show off various construction projects he's led,
including the helipad and upcoming ballroom.
Trump said next year's turkey pardon will be held
in the new ballroom.
Franco Ordonez, NPR News, the White House.
>> The S&P 500 was off 36 points today.
The Dow gained 423, closing at 50,000, 18.
This is NPR News in Washington.
Armed men are holding hostages inside a supermarket
in the Colombian tourist city
of Cartagena, John Otis reports.
>> President Abelardo de la Esprella described the kidnappers
as common criminals who took refuge inside a supermarket
after they failed to rob cash from an armored truck.
Police have surrounded the supermarket
while inside government envoys are negotiating
with the criminals.
Speaking at a news conference, the president predicted
that the standoff would end well for the hostages,
but not so well for the hostage takers.
The kidnappings occurred on the 10th anniversary
of a peace treaty that disarmed Colombia's largest guerrilla
group, but a new generation
of drug trafficking rebels is now carrying out attacks
in many parts of the country.
For NPR News, I'm John Otis in Bogota, Colombia.
>> A Cessna 210 this afternoon went down in the Gulf of Mexico
between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island.
Rescue crews are searching
for the six people aboard, including two children.
Responders did find life jackets, a life raft,
and the plane's cabin floating but no passengers.
A flight tracking website indicates the small plane was
on route from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida.
In the San Francisco Bay area, people are on alert

The Pacific Northwest and parts
